source.citation: Crawford JR, Howell DC. Comparing an individual's test score against norms derived from small samples. Clin Neuropsychol 1998;12(4):482-486. doi:10.1076/clin.12.4.482.7241
source.note: The paper's modified t-test, after Sokal & Rohlf (1995): t = (X1 - mean2) / (s2 x sqrt((N2 + 1) / N2)) with df = N2 - 1, where s2 is the sample SD (N - 1) of the comparison sample (p. 483). This article is not in PubMed; the citation was checked against Crossref and the authors' PDF.

rci.method: t = (today's value - baseline mean) / (baseline SD x sqrt(1 + 1/n)), with n baseline days, the sample SD (n - 1) and df = n - 1. A reliable change is |t| above the two-tailed critical value of Student's t at alpha 0.001 with n - 1 degrees of freedom: 4.221 for a full 14-day baseline, 5.959 at the 7-day minimum. An indicator that declares a transform is tested on that scale: PVT-B lapses, a count, on the Anscombe transform 2√(x + 3/8) of every value, with the band mapped back to lapses. No test-retest reliability is used.

lineage.text: The question, whether a change is bigger than day-to-day noise, is Jacobson & Truax's 'reliable change'. Their arithmetic divides by a reference-group SD and a published test-retest reliability. LANDFALL compares each crewmember with their own baseline, whose SD already contains the day-to-day noise, so it uses Crawford & Howell's single-case test instead.

source.citation: Jacobson NS, Truax P. Clinical significance: a statistical approach to defining meaningful change in psychotherapy research. J Consult Clin Psychol 1991;59(1):12-19. doi:10.1037//0022-006x.59.1.12. PMID 2002127

source.rationale: Stricter than the conventional 0.05 because LANDFALL tests many indicators every day. With the single-case t-test this is the actual chance rate per indicator-day under normal, independent day-to-day noise (half of it for a change in the worse direction), and the expected rate is printed next to every personal finding: the nominal one, or, for an indicator whose measured rate under the scenario's noise model is not within 0.5-2 times it, the measured one, which that indicator declares.
Seven baseline days is the fewest we accept for a sample SD; with fewer, the finding reports insufficient data.
Two weeks of the crewmember's own data, long enough to span weekday/weekend schedule differences.

rci.caveat: The chance rate is exactly alpha (0.001 two-tailed, 0.0005 for a change in the worse direction) per indicator-day only if day-to-day noise is normal and independent, and real data are neither. In seeded simulations with no real change, laid out like the scenario (a fixed 14-day baseline, then each of the 31 days after it tested against it), lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.5 between days gave about 1.4 times alpha on the first day after the baseline, about 4 times from a week on, and about 3.7 times averaged over the 31 days. At 0.9 it gave about 2.5 times on the first day and about 67 times on average, because 14 strongly autocorrelated days under-sample the crewmember's usual range. Skewed counts tested as raw counts (Poisson with mean 1, like PVT-B lapses) gave about 5 times alpha, and every one of those chance flags was a rise, so the chance-caution rate was about 10 times the printed one; LANDFALL therefore tests counts on the Anscombe scale (an indicator's transform), where PVT-B lapses flag about half as often as printed instead. Crawford et al. 2006 likewise saw this test's rate reach 9.96% against a nominal 5% with skewed, heavy-tailed samples. The rate of every indicator under the scenario's own noise model is measured, not assumed, and published with the simulated scenario data: an indicator whose measured rate is not within 0.5 to 2 times the nominal one declares its measured rate, and LANDFALL prints that instead. That noise model has no autocorrelation; real days do, so for real data read every printed rate, nominal or measured, as a lower bound.

caveat_basis.text: Monte Carlo study of Crawford & Howell's test with non-normal control samples: leptokurtosis alone inflated the Type I error only modestly; leptokurtosis with skew gave actual rates as high as 9.96% against a specified 5% at small sample sizes (abstract).

source.citation: Crawford JR, Garthwaite PH, Azzalini A, Howell DC, Laws KR. Testing for a deficit in single-case studies: effects of departures from normality. Neuropsychologia 2006;44(4):666-677. doi:10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2005.06.001. PMID 16046228

rci.change_note: An earlier version applied Jacobson & Truax's arithmetic (a standard error of the difference of SD x sqrt(2) x sqrt(1 - r), critical 3.29) to the crewmember's own baseline SD. An audit showed that this shrinks the denominator: with a 14-day baseline and r = 0.8 the chance-flag rate was about 6.6% per indicator-day, not the 0.1% printed. Tier B now uses Crawford & Howell's test, whose chance rate is alpha. A later audit, after the scenario's day-to-day noise was made realistic, found two indicators far above the printed rate: the absolute sleep midpoint shift (a folded, in-sample-centred variable; about 12.7 times the printed caution rate) and raw PVT-B lapse counts (about 10 times). The midpoint is now a signed shift tested in both directions, and counts are tested on the Anscombe scale.

detectable_change.text: The smallest one-day change Tier B can flag is the band's half-width, critical x baseline SD x sqrt(1 + 1/n), and every Tier B finding reports it. With a full 14-day baseline that is 4.37 baseline SDs; at the 7-day minimum, 6.37. A real change smaller than that is never flagged, however much it matters: Tier B's sensitivity is set by the crewmember's own day-to-day noise. For an indicator with a transform (PVT-B lapses) the SDs are on the transformed scale, and the band is printed mapped back to the indicator's own unit.

source.arithmetic: critical t (two-tailed alpha 0.001, df 13) x sqrt(1 + 1/14) = 4.221 x 1.035 = 4.37; critical t (df 6) x sqrt(1 + 1/7) = 5.959 x 1.069 = 6.37

definition.text: lapse = reaction time ≥ 355 ms on the 3-min PVT-B

source.citation: Basner M, Mollicone D, Dinges DF. Validity and sensitivity of a brief psychomotor vigilance test (PVT-B) to total and partial sleep deprivation. Acta Astronaut 2011;69(11-12):949-959. doi:10.1016/j.actaastro.2011.07.015. PMID 22025811
source.note: Basner 2011 generated PVT-B lapses at 355 ms as a sixth outcome variable, alongside lapses at the standard 500 ms; the authors note the 355 ms threshold 'was found post-hoc in the TSD experiment, and may depend on PVT hardware'. No NASA standard or brief adopts 355 ms.

transform_basis.text: PVT-B lapses are a small count (about 1 per rested 3-minute test), whose day-to-day noise is skewed: on the raw counts the single-case test raised a chance caution about 10 times as often as printed. Tier B therefore tests the Anscombe transform of the count, y = 2√(x + 3/8), which makes a Poisson count's variance roughly constant, against the same transform of every baseline value. The personal band is computed on that scale and mapped back to counts, x = (y/2)² - 3/8, so the crew sees it in lapses; the transform is monotone, so a count is outside that band exactly when its transform is outside the band of the test.

source.citation: Anscombe FJ. The transformation of Poisson, binomial and negative-binomial data. Biometrika 1948;35(3-4):246-254. doi:10.1093/biomet/35.3-4.246
source.note: Bibliographic record checked against Crossref (DOI 10.1093/biomet/35.3-4.246) on 2026-11-14. 2√(x + 3/8) is the form of the transform that gives a variance close to 1 for large means; at a mean near 1 count the transformed variance is lower, which is why its measured chance rate is reported.

chance_rate.text: Measured, not assumed: with no real change under the scenario's noise model (one Poisson count per test, mean 0.9-1.2 lapses), a seeded Monte Carlo laid out like the scenario (620,000 tests: a fixed 14-day baseline, then 31 days each tested against it) on the Anscombe scale raised a caution 0.45 times as often as the printed alpha/2 (0.34-0.52 across the four crewmembers) and a flag in either direction 0.24 times as often as alpha. A count near zero can never fall reliably, and the transform slightly over-corrects so small a count, so under that model lapses flag less often than the nominal rate, and LANDFALL prints this measured rate instead. The model's days are independent; real days are not, so for real data read this rate as a lower bound, like every printed rate.

source.arithmetic: caution multiplier = 141 worse-direction reliable changes / 620,000 tests / 0.0005 = 0.45; flag multiplier = 150 reliable changes in either direction / 620,000 tests / 0.001 = 0.24 (seeded Monte Carlo with the scenario generator's noise model, 5,000 simulated 45-day records per crewmember)
source.note: The engine's own tests replay this study and require these values; the same study, for every indicator, is published with the simulated scenario data.

definition.text: signed shift, in hours, of the night's sleep midpoint from the median sleep midpoint of the crewmember's fixed baseline window (the window Tier B uses; MET days 368-381 in the demo scenario), with clock arithmetic across midnight and wrapped to [-12, 12) h: positive is later, negative is earlier. A shift either way is worse, so a reliable change in either direction raises a caution

source.rationale: A signed shift from a fixed reference keeps the day-to-day noise of the midpoint itself: subtracting the baseline median moves every value by the same amount, so the single-case test sees the midpoint's own spread and its chance rate is the printed one. An earlier version tested the absolute shift, which folds the noise at zero and centres it on the baseline's own median; with no real change it raised a chance caution about 12 times as often as printed (seeded Monte Carlo under the scenario's noise model). As for glucose, worse is either: an earlier or a later midpoint is a drift, and the chance-caution rate of a two-sided indicator is alpha, not alpha/2, and LANDFALL's false-alarm arithmetic counts it that way.
